vignette:
Sarah is a thirty-five-year-old actor who has spent the last eight months feeling as though she is living behind a pane of glass, watching a life that is no longer hers. The change began on a Tuesday afternoon on a crowded subway car. The memory itself is not a story she can tell; it comes in flashes, disconnected pieces that refuse to form a coherent narrative. There is the high-pitched screech of the train’s brakes between stations, the sudden pop-pop-pop that she first thought was fireworks, the glint of something metallic under the harsh fluorescent lights. She remembers a man in a dark, tactical-style jacket—something that looked almost like a uniform—and the way people dropped to the floor around her. She can’t seem to put the sequence of events into words, but when a memory fragment does surface, it isn’t a thought but a full-body experience. The floor of her apartment will suddenly feel like it is vibrating, the air will thicken with a coppery smell, and she is right back in that subway car, her heart hammering against her ribs as if it is happening for the first time.

In the weeks that followed the incident, her world began to shrink. The subway, once a daily necessity for auditions and rehearsals, became an impossible space. Just the thought of descending the stairs into a station, of the sealed doors closing her in, was enough to trigger a wave of nausea. She started taking rideshares everywhere, a habit that quickly drained her savings. This financial pressure was compounded by a new, almost compulsive need to spend money. When the strong, undifferentiated feelings of horror and shame would wash over her, she would find herself online, her cart filling with expensive clothes and skincare products she didn't need. The brief thrill of the purchase was the only thing that seemed to quiet the noise in her head, if only for a moment.

Her career, which had been gaining momentum, has stalled. Three months ago, she walked into an audition for a small role on a police procedural. The moment she saw the lead actor in his police costume, holding a prop firearm, the casting room dissolved. She was no longer in a studio but back in the chaos, the sounds of the director giving notes replaced by muffled screaming. She mumbled an apology and fled, leaving her agent to clean up the mess. Since then, she avoids any project that might involve police, military, or action sequences. This has severely limited her opportunities, feeding a growing sense of professional despair. She has come to believe she is permanently an outsider now, set apart from her peers who can navigate these make-believe worlds without being pulled back into a real one. This feeling of isolation is pervasive. When she is with friends, she finds herself scanning the restaurant, her back always to a wall, her eyes tracking the exits. She is constantly choosing where to sit based on how safe or protected she feels, a logic no one else seems to operate by. Her ex-boyfriend used to tell her, "You're safe here with me," but the words were meaningless. She has found it impossible to believe in safety, even when it is promised.

The knowledge that the shooter was never caught has become a source of profound anger and fear. She obsessively followed the news for months, waiting for a resolution that never came. This lack of accountability has cemented a belief that the world is fundamentally unjust and dangerous. It is this feeling, more than anything, that has finally brought her to therapy. Her life has become a series of strategic retreats, her apartment a fortress against a city she once loved. She feels utterly alone, cut off from her friends, her work, and her own sense of self. She hopes therapy can help her find a way back, but what frightens her most is the thought that this feeling of being set apart, of being a perpetual witness to a danger no one else can see, might be permanent.
